summary: An experimental protocol layered on HTTP that lets a server hold several versions of the same resource under one URL, such as different languages or formats, and pick the best one for each client automatically. The aim was to make it easier to roll out new data formats and markup.

plainLanguage.summary: Transparent content negotiation lets one HTTP resource have several versions, such as different languages or media types. The server can list the versions for the user agent to choose, or return a suitable version directly when the user agent permits it.

questions: how does http choose between variants
what does the alternates header do
what is http status 506 variant also negotiates
subtitle: An experimental HTTP extension for choosing among multiple representations of one resource.

tldr.problem: A resource may have several representations, but sending a long list of client capabilities with every request can be inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: The server can return an Alternates list for the user agent to choose from, or make a choice on its behalf when an agreed remote selection algorithm has enough information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2295 is an Experimental extension to HTTP with new headers and status code 506. It defines no remote variant selection algorithm itself.

today: RFC 2295 is an Experimental document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It names RFC 2296 as a companion for a remote selection algorithm, but RFC 2295 itself defines no such algorithm.

sections.title: One Resource with Several Variants
sections.content:
RFC 2295 defines transparent content negotiation as an extension on top of HTTP. A single URI can have several representations, called variants, and a user agent can retrieve a suitable one using GET or HEAD. The variants are visible to outside parties through a machine-readable list.

The RFC describes possible uses such as selecting media type, character set, language, or features supported by a user agent. Content encoding is outside the negotiation dimensions defined here. The memo is Experimental and does not specify an Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: A website can associate several versions of a resource with one address. This extension describes how a user agent and server select one of those versions.

sections.title: The List and Choice Exchange
sections.content:
In the basic exchange, the server returns a list response containing an Alternates header with descriptions of the available variants. The user agent selects one and sends an ordinary HTTP request for that variant. A list response may also include a body that lets a person choose manually.

To avoid a second request, a user agent may send small Accept headers and allow a remote variant selection algorithm. If the server or a proxy has enough information and the selected variant is neighboring, it can return a choice response directly. The user agent must permit the algorithm through its Negotiate request header.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can show a list and let the user agent request its chosen version. If the user agent allows a selection algorithm and the server has enough information, the server can return the chosen version directly.

sections.title: Variant Descriptions and Features
sections.content:
A variant description gives the variant URI and a source-quality value, with optional attributes such as media type, charset, language, length, and features. Source quality describes the representation before the user agent renders it. The RFC advises that file size belongs in the length attribute rather than in source quality.

Feature tags can describe capabilities or preferences beyond media type, charset, and language, such as tables or color depth. Predicates in the features attribute affect the variant's quality according to whether a feature is present and, when applicable, its value. This specification does not define feature tags.
sections.plainLanguage: Each variant can list its format, language, size, and other properties. Feature tags let the selection process account for additional capabilities or preferences.

sections.title: Headers and Status Code
sections.content:
The extension defines the Negotiate request header, the Alternates response header, the TCN response header, Accept-Features, and Variant-Vary. TCN identifies a list, choice, or adhoc response. Alternates carries the variant list, while Negotiate tells the server which negotiation behavior the user agent supports or allows.

Status code 506, Variant Also Negotiates, reports a server configuration error: the selected variant is itself configured for transparent negotiation and therefore is not an endpoint for the current negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The new headers tell the parties what variants exist and what kind of negotiation response was returned. Status 506 means the selected variant is incorrectly configured to negotiate again.

sections.title: Caching and User-Agent Behavior
sections.content:
Negotiated responses use TCN to identify their response type and Vary information to support correct cache handling. Structured entity tags can carry both a validator for the response and a validator for the variant list. Proxies may reuse an Alternates header or extract a normal response from a choice response when the rules permit it.

Transparent negotiation applies to GET and HEAD, not directly to the result of a POST. A POST may instead return a redirect that leads to a resource fetched with GET. User agents should be able to show the variant list and allow a person to review choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Responses need cache information so a proxy does not serve the wrong variant. The negotiation applies to GET and HEAD requests, while a POST can redirect to a later GET.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Accept headers, especially Accept-Language, may reveal information a user would prefer not to share. Even when those headers are omitted, the variant selected by the user agent can reveal a preference. The RFC describes a malicious server that could offer false language variants to infer sensitive information.

A cache may also be affected if a negotiated resource controls responses for neighboring variants created by another author. The RFC says servers need to filter Content-Location values in choice responses. Negotiation may also expose security weaknesses in user agents, such as support for scripting languages or libraries.
sections.plainLanguage: A language or format choice can reveal information about the user, even when preference headers are omitted. Servers and caches also need safeguards so one resource cannot control another author's variant.
